A 2024 systematic review and meta-analysis included 18 articles and 31,203 participants. For the general child population, pooled prevalence was 5%.
Meta-analysis subgroups:

The 5% figure is a synthesis of studies of the general child population. The subgroups by sex and region help explore variation, but high heterogeneity means they should not be treated as definitive geographical differences.
Cite 5% as pooled childhood prevalence from the meta-analysis. Regional figures are subgroups with high heterogeneity and should not be used to rank continents.
Heterogeneity between studies was very high. Regional differences come from few studies and should not be used as a geographical ranking.

The figures
CDC summarises studies that include diagnosed and undiagnosed children and estimates that approximately 1 in 162 children (0.6%) have Tourette syndrome.
In the United States, parent-reported diagnosis data were lower:
in children aged 3 to 17, approximately 174,000 children in the 2016–2019 period.

This page contrasts two ways of measuring: studies that try to capture diagnosed and undiagnosed cases, and a U.S. survey based on parent-reported diagnosis. The difference between 0.6% and 0.3% illustrates why prevalence and recorded identification are not synonyms.
Estimated prevalence from active studies may be higher than the number of recorded diagnoses. Identification and prevalence are not synonyms.
Distinguish between the estimate from studies that include diagnosed and undiagnosed cases (0.6%) and parent-reported diagnosis in the U.S. (0.3%).

The figures
A widely cited British population study estimated a prevalence of 7.58% for language disorder of then-unknown origin in children entering school.

The 7.58% figure comes from a British population study of children entering school. It is useful because it clearly defines the population studied, but it was not designed as a representative estimate for every country in the world.
Cite 7.58% as the result of a British population study of children entering school. Do not label it as global prevalence of DLD.
